claim_text: The UFLPA presumption reaches goods mined, produced or manufactured 'wholly or in part' in the XUAR or by a listed entity, and an exception requires the importer to have fully complied with FLETF guidance, answered all CBP inquiries, and shown by clear and convincing evidence that no forced labor was used.
notes: The 'wholly or in part' wording is what makes tier depth a live design question: the statute sets no tier limit, so the effective depth is set by guidance and enforcement practice.

claim_text: CBP's June 2022 operational guidance asked polysilicon importers for a flow chart running from the location of the quartzite through the polysilicon plant to downstream facilities, and warned that factories sourcing both XUAR and non-XUAR polysilicon risk detention because commingling is hard to rule out.
notes: On paper the documentation expectation for solar goes to the raw-material tier (quartz), i.e. beyond the spec's E3 position.

claim_text: CBP's June 2026 consolidated guidance keeps the same quartzite-to-import mapping and commingling warning for 'silica-based products (including polysilicon)'; the documentary tracing depth expected for solar was neither narrowed nor widened between 2022 and 2026.
counter_evidence: Unchanged wording does not mean unchanged practice: what CBP actually accepts in applicability reviews is not public, and practitioner reports (EV-038) describe stricter handling of extensions in 2025.
notes: Medium because the 'neither narrowed nor widened' part is our comparison of two primary texts, not a CBP statement.

claim_text: The FLETF Strategy (June 2022) tells importers to be able to trace the complete supply chain 'from raw materials to finished good', and allows DNA or isotopic origin testing as evidence if its reliability is demonstrated.

CBP says importers can cut detention of shipments from a previously cleared supply chain (including commingled ones) to an average of 10-14 days by filing a summary tracing report naming suppliers at every production stage.
notes: This lowers the cost of meeting deep tracing for repeat importers, which matters for how disruptive a deeper tier setting would be.

claim_text: CBP's summary-tracing-report shortcut resembles what ACP asked for in March 2022, namely that a source already shown XUAR-free should not be re-examined in each detention. This is consistent with industry input shaping how the tracing burden is processed, not how deep it goes.
counter_evidence: CBP has its own workload reasons to reuse prior reviews (see capacity claims C-033, C-034); no document links the FAQ to the ACP comment.
notes: Our inference from timing and content only.

claim_text: In its March 2022 FLETF comment SEIA argued that leading importers had already shown CBP by clear and convincing evidence that their panels were free of XUAR inputs under the Hoshine WRO, and proposed recognising 'verified' importers and using information requests (CF-28) or RASA reviews before any detention.
notes: Confidence refers to the record of what SEIA said, not to whether the claim about importers was true. SEIA's 2022 membership included US arms of Chinese module makers (reported, not verified here).

claim_text: ACP told the FLETF in March 2022 that under the Hoshine WRO, CBP detained all imports of suppliers accounting for about two-thirds of US modules from August 2021 by classifying their whole output as high risk, and asked for process changes so cleared sources are not re-examined and detentions do not rest on outdated information.
notes: Position by an industry association. The two-thirds figure is ACP's and is not independently verified.

claim_text: First Solar, a US thin-film maker that does not use polysilicon, urged the FLETF in March 2022 to scrutinise manufacturers with long-term supply agreements with XUAR polysilicon producers (or producers with XUAR subsidiaries) and those tied to BIS Entity List firms, and noted that polysilicon blending and multiple bills of materials per module model make tracing hard.
notes: First Solar's 10-K (EV-026) says it competes partly on responsible sourcing against crystalline-silicon makers mostly linked to China, so it benefits commercially from a wider trigger and ownership reach. That is a commercial interest, not evidence of bad faith.

claim_text: First Solar's FY2025 10-K states it does not use polysilicon, which limits its UFLPA disruption risk, and that its main competitors are crystalline-silicon module makers 'the majority of which are linked to China'.
notes: Formal submission; reliable for what the company disclosed.

claim_text: The initial June 2022 UFLPA Entity List (20 entities) was drawn from existing CBP Withhold Release Orders and the Commerce BIS Entity List, not from entities named only in research.

In July 2022 Reuters reported that lawmakers had asked CBP to explain why three major Chinese solar companies were left off the list, noting that a wider scope could threaten US panel supply and the administration's decarbonisation goal; a senior Labor Department official acknowledged 'competing objectives within an administration'.
counter_evidence: The official's remark is general and does not mention solar; she declined to comment on the solar companies. The lawmakers' letter itself was not located.
notes: Single secondary source. The underlying letter would raise this to high.

claim_text: The record is consistent with a deliberate choice in 2022-2024 to keep the largest crystalline-silicon module brands off the Entity List and handle them shipment by shipment through detentions instead: the boundary was publicly contested (C-012), and the FLETF says it prioritised entities that 'egregiously, and with corroborated evidence' met the listing criteria (C-014).
counter_evidence: Other explanations: (1) the evidentiary bar of 'reasonable cause based on specific and articulable information' and APA review of listings (C-035); (2) major brands built separate US-bound non-XUAR lines (C-030), which may have removed the factual basis for listing; (3) staff limits on case building (C-033).
notes: Allowed only as 'consistent with'. It still needs a Layer 3 data cliff on the trigger_scope dial before it can be shown; mark as pending until the exposure curve is computed.

claim_text: The FLETF's 2024 strategy update says the list grew from 20 to 68 entities, that it 'prioritized its efforts to identify entities who have egregiously, and with corroborated evidence' met the criteria, and that it had built a 'scalable' process to list entities faster.

The January 15 2025 additions (37 entities, bringing the total to 144) included Donghai JA Solar Technology in Jiangsu, listed under section 2(d)(2)(B)(v) for sourcing polysilicon from an XUAR producer, along with Hongyuan Green Energy and its Inner Mongolia subsidiary and Shuangliang Silicon. These are non-XUAR solar wafer, cell and module firms reached through their polysilicon sourcing.
notes: Shows the list moving from XUAR-based producers toward non-XUAR downstream solar firms through clause (v).

claim_text: No entities were added to the UFLPA Entity List between January 15 2025 and August 3 2026: the August 2026 notice expressly supersedes the list published on January 15 2025.
notes: The 19-month freeze is the main timing feature of the trigger_scope dial.

claim_text: On August 3 2026 the FLETF added 43 entities (total 187), the largest single expansion so far, aimed mainly at aluminum, apparel, copper, cotton and tomato supply chains. TBEA, which also makes high-purity polysilicon, was listed on the stated basis that it sources aluminum and its subsidiary Tianchi Energy sources coal from the XUAR. The notice also renamed listed polysilicon maker Xinjiang GCL as Xinjiang Goens Energy Technology.
notes: DHS framed the additions partly as protecting 'American businesses from foreign competitors' unfair practices' (EV-022).

claim_text: Because the presumption attaches to goods 'produced by' a listed entity whatever the listing rationale, TBEA's own polysilicon now falls within scope even though TBEA was listed for aluminum and coal. The extracted notice text does not show whether TBEA's polysilicon subsidiary Xinte Energy was named, so that output may sit outside the list unless it is covered by the XUAR-origin prong.
counter_evidence: Xinte's production is in the XUAR, so its polysilicon is presumptively barred under the geographic prong anyway; the ownership gap mainly matters for non-XUAR affiliates.
notes: Reasonable reading of primary documents. Open question: check the full appendix for Xinte (the other agent's entity_list_history.csv may resolve this).

claim_text: The UFLPA list covers named entities only: subsidiaries are added by name (e.g. Tianshan Aluminum 'and the seven named subsidiaries' in August 2026), and since May 16 2024 the FLETF counts each named subsidiary or affiliate as a separate entity. We found no rule extending the presumption to unnamed affiliates.
counter_evidence: Absence of evidence: the statute and notices do not explicitly exclude affiliates; CBP can still target affiliates as a risk factor (C-020).
notes: The naming practice is high confidence; 'no affiliate rule' is our reading of the primary documents, so medium overall.

claim_text: The FLETF's 2023 strategy update says CBP prioritises imports from non-XUAR entities that are related to an XUAR entity (as parent, subsidiary or affiliate) and are also likely to contain XUAR inputs. Ownership is a targeting factor for detentions, not an automatic trigger of the presumption.
notes: Supports the spec default of ownership reach 'Off' for the legal presumption, with A1 approximating CBP's risk targeting rather than the law.

claim_text: The 2021 Hoshine WRO, the predecessor action for solar, expressly covered Hoshine 'and its subsidiaries' and goods such as polysilicon derived from its silica-based products.
notes: Ownership and derived-input reach were built into the solar enforcement tool before the UFLPA list existed.

claim_text: Commerce's BIS adopted a 50% 'Affiliates Rule' for its own Entity List on September 30 2025, suspended it from November 10 2025 to November 9 2026, and scheduled it to come back on November 10 2026. No equivalent 50% rule exists for the UFLPA Entity List.
counter_evidence: Whether the BIS rule actually resumed on 2026-11-10 was not verified.
notes: Comparator only: the BIS rule does not change UFLPA scope. The 'no equivalent' part rests on our search of DHS/CBP materials.

claim_text: Between June 21 and October 25 2022 CBP detained 1,053 shipments of solar equipment and released none (public-records response to Reuters). ACP reported a 23% fall in Q3 2022 installations and about 23 GW of projects delayed, largely from lack of panels.
counter_evidence: ACP figures are an industry estimate; other factors (the 2022 Commerce anti-circumvention inquiry, logistics) also hit module supply in 2022.
notes: CSIS (EV-035) independently reports >1,000 electronics stops in Q3 2022, mostly solar, 69% from Malaysia/Vietnam.

claim_text: By March 2023 module imports were flowing again; White House adviser John Podesta attributed this to 'clearer guidance', and Trina said more than 900 MW had cleared in four months with under 1% detained.
counter_evidence: Supplier shifts to separate non-XUAR lines (C-030) may explain the thaw as much as clearer guidance.
notes: Single secondary source quoting officials and a company.

claim_text: Of the $3.94bn in shipments stopped under the UFLPA since 2022, HTS 8541 (which includes solar cells and modules) accounts for $3.26bn (82%), and more than 79% of that value was later released. Total stopped value fell from $1.78bn in 2024 to $187.7m in 2025.
counter_evidence: HTS 8541 also includes LEDs and other semiconductor devices, so 8541 is an upper bound for solar. Dashboard definitions changed in 2026 (C-027).
notes: Reuters analysis of CBP data, corroborated by ArentFox Schiff (8541 >61% of FY2025 value). The high release share suggests most solar stops end in applicability/admissibility clearance, not exclusion.

claim_text: According to a December 2025 letter from House Democrats citing CBP data, monthly stopped shipments averaged 1,062 from November 2024 to March 2025 and 224 from April to August 2025, against averages of 334 (2023) and 383 (2024).
counter_evidence: Law-firm tallies show FY2025 detentions above FY2024 by count (driven by the early-FY2025 peak), and the April 2025 shift to immediate exclusions (C-027) changes what is counted.
notes: Partisan source quoting official data. CRS (EV-030) confirms the letter and the concern about a relative decline in 2025.

claim_text: UFLPA shipment counts are not comparable across sources or over time. The 2026 dashboard counts each import transaction line and treats 'stopped' as an automated hold, not necessarily a physical detention (65,707 stopped by November 2025, against roughly 16,700 'shipments' under the older method). From April 2025 CBP also sometimes excluded goods immediately instead of detaining them first.
notes: This is a data limit that cuts against reading any count-based 'slowdown' or 'surge' as a change in policy. Value-based series are more robust.

claim_text: Reps. DeLauro, Krishnamoorthi and colleagues suggested that the 2025 drop in UFLPA enforcement may reflect CBP resources diverted to tariff implementation and cuts to forced-labor programmes at TIP, DRL and ILAB, and asked why no entities had been added since January 15 2025.
counter_evidence: DHS's response, if any, was not found.
notes: Partisan letter; confidence refers to what was asked or argued.

claim_text: In August 2025 a former CBP enforcement attorney (now general counsel at LONGi) said CBP had lost talent and senior attorneys in 2025, that its resources were 'stretched' by tariff and traceability demands, and that the Electronics Center had stopped granting extensions for UFLPA document packages.
counter_evidence: The speaker works for a major Chinese module maker affected by UFLPA enforcement.
notes: Single secondary source, interested party. Treat as a lead, not an established fact.

claim_text: Independent research agrees the UFLPA pushed polysilicon sourcing for US-bound solar out of the XUAR but not the upstream MGS/quartz tiers. The XUAR's share of solar-grade polysilicon fell from about 45% (2020) to about 35% (2022) and about 25% of capacity (2025), while its share of China's metallurgical-grade silicon rose to about 53%. Major makers run separate US-bound lines.
counter_evidence: Market shares come mainly from one analyst (Bernreuter) cited by both CSIS and Sheffield Hallam, so the two sources are not fully independent on the numbers.
notes: Supports placing the main residual exposure at tiers 3-4 (MGS, quartz) for the Layer 3 model.

claim_text: The remaining XUAR exposure in US solar imports is concentrated at the MGS/quartz tiers, where verification is hardest, so a tier-depth step from polysilicon (E2) to MGS/quartz (E3) is the most likely place for a 'cliff' in the exposure curve.
counter_evidence: CBP guidance nominally already requires quartzite-level mapping (C-002, C-003), so any gap is in verification and enforcement practice rather than the written rule. RAND notes its tier counts may reflect better data rather than more exposure.
notes: Our hypothesis to test against the Layer 3 data, not a finding.

claim_text: RAND found that the number of US businesses with second- to fourth-tier customer links to XUAR entities persisted or grew after the UFLPA, and that the share of shipments from XUAR-connected foreign firms stayed roughly constant, even as direct shipments largely stopped.
counter_evidence: RAND itself cautions the apparent increase may reflect better data collection and reporting on XUAR links.
notes: Single independent study, across all products rather than solar specifically.

claim_text: CBP capacity has been a recorded limit throughout. Before the UFLPA, GAO found staff shortages had suspended some forced-labor investigations. Congress then funded about 338 UFLPA/forced-labor positions in FY2022-23, and in FY2026 directed CBP to keep forced-labor funding at no less than FY2025 levels.
notes: The capacity explanation applies to every dial: deeper tiers, wider triggers and ownership reach all multiply review workload.

claim_text: CSIS judged in 2023 that even with the added resources, stopping goods across all the product categories and companies named in research would be 'an impossible task for CBP'. This is a capacity argument against a research-named (R1) trigger.
counter_evidence: Advocates (EV-042, EV-043) argue a broader list improves compliance without extra port workload because importers self-police.
notes: Independent analysis; medium for the reasoning, which is consistent with the GAO capacity record (C-033).

claim_text: Entity List decisions face judicial review under the APA. In Camel Group (Slip Op. 26-95, 2026) the Court of International Trade sent the FLETF's refusal to delist back to the agency for lack of reasoned decision-making, without vacating it, following Ninestar.
notes: A legal constraint: each listing needs a documented, reasoned record, which limits how fast and on what evidence (e.g. research-only naming) the list can grow.

claim_text: On August 5 2026, two days after the expansion took effect, China's Commerce Ministry put six US organisations on its countermeasures list, including supply-chain mapping, audit and origin-testing providers (Altana, the Responsible Business Alliance, Verite, Applied DNA Sciences). Firms in China may not transact with them.
notes: Single law-firm source. If confirmed, this is a legal constraint on importers' ability to produce upstream (MGS/quartz) evidence, independent of US choices.

claim_text: Human Rights Watch argued in 2022 that 'clear and convincing evidence' is 'a near impossible bar' for XUAR-linked sourcing because surveillance and threats prevent meaningful audits, and that companies should exit rather than audit.
notes: Advocacy position; confidence refers to the record of what was said.

claim_text: Independent and advocacy sources attribute the 2025 enforcement decline and the static list to weak political will. CSIS (2025) said it had 'not yet seen a commitment' from the new administration, and the Coalition said a 'static list' forecloses use of the presumption.
counter_evidence: Several things point the other way: the same administration added five high-priority sectors (August 2025) and made the largest-ever list expansion (August 2026); capacity diversion (C-028, C-029) and counting changes (C-027) also fit the data.
notes: Confidence refers to the positions being stated.

claim_text: On balance the 2025 slowdown fits capacity diversion, staff loss and process or counting changes better than a decision to narrow the UFLPA's boundaries, because the written boundaries (tracing guidance, sectors) held or widened over 2025-2026 and the list later grew sharply.
counter_evidence: Political-will explanations (C-038) and US-China trade negotiations (the BIS affiliates suspension, C-022, came out of trade talks according to secondary reporting not read here) cannot be ruled out; there is no document stating why no listings were made between January 2025 and August 2026.
notes: Our inference. Never framed as intent.

claim_text: Maxeon disclosed that CBP had detained its US solar imports since July 2024, that a $614.1m revenue fall was mainly due to the detentions, and that CBP denied its protests in late March 2025, leaving the goods excluded and prompting a Court of International Trade challenge. Solar detentions of established brands continued through the 2025 lull.
notes: Company securities filing: reliable for what was disclosed, but the company's account of compliance is self-interested. 'Continued through the lull' is our reading.

claim_text: Solar targeting in 2024-2025 was driven in part by information from questionnaires CBP sent to large solar importers in early 2024.
notes: Two independent practitioner sources agree; the questionnaire itself is not public.

claim_text: SEIA's ANSI/SEIA 101 standard, built on examples of solar shipments CBP detained and released, sets traceability 'from raw materials to finished goods'. The industry is aligning its own standard with the depth CBP enforces rather than arguing for a shallower one.
counter_evidence: The standard's actual depth (whether it reaches MGS and quartz) was not checked; the standard text is not public.
notes: Confidence refers to what SEIA stated; the interpretive half is low.
